posts.headline: Uniform excellence should not depend on which city you practise in
posts.sub: A consultant in a district town and one in a metro should be able to reach the same standard of care. That is the whole point of what we build.
posts.caption:
Continuing education in India is not short of lectures. What it is short of is continuity, a structured path through one skill, taught in the same voice, session after session, so that what a clinician learns in the third hour builds on the first.

All India CME is being built as that path rather than as a series of one-off talks. Each programme is CME taught the masterclass way: one clinical skill, a curriculum that progresses, and a standard that does not vary with geography.

Uniform excellence in clinical practice is not a slogan for us. It is the test we apply to every session that goes on the calendar, and the reason we would rather run fewer sessions well than many indifferently.

posts.sub: A year-long CME programme in pain management moves from assessment and pharmacology to interventional technique, and each session assumes the one before it.
posts.caption:
Two hours on a Sunday can introduce a topic. It cannot build a skill. The gap between knowing about pain management and practising it well is a matter of sequence: assessment before pharmacology, pharmacology before blocks, and supervised clinical reasoning threaded through all of it.

That is why the longer programmes are structured as CME in masterclass format, twenty-four sessions across a year, one skill, each session written on the assumption that the previous one landed. Attendance at session nineteen should mean something different from attendance at session one.

posts.headline: A strong recommendation can still rest on moderate certainty
posts.sub: Strength tells you how confidently to act. Certainty tells you how solid the underlying evidence is. Guidelines label both, and the two do not always move together.
posts.caption:
Two labels sit next to most modern recommendations, and they answer different questions. Strength, strong or conditional, is guidance on action: how confidently should a clinician do this for most patients. Certainty, high through very low, is a verdict on the evidence itself.

They come apart more often than people expect. A strong recommendation on moderate certainty usually means the benefit is large and consistent enough to act on even though the trials are imperfect. A conditional recommendation on the same certainty usually means the evidence is reasonable but the balance of benefit and burden depends on the patient in front of you.

Reading both labels, and not just the verb in the sentence, is the difference between following a guideline and using one.

posts.headline: Non-severe TB in a child: does treatment still have to run six months?
posts.sub: WHO 2022 recommends four months, not six, between 3 months and 16 years of age, when disease is non-severe and drug resistance is neither suspected nor evident.
posts.caption:
Ask this in a busy clinic and the reflex answer is six months. The current WHO consolidated guidance on tuberculosis says otherwise for a defined group: in children and adolescents between 3 months and 16 years of age with non-severe disease, and without suspicion or evidence of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis, a four-month regimen should be used. It is a strong recommendation on moderate certainty evidence.

The caveat is the whole recommendation. Non-severe here means peripheral lymph node disease, intrathoracic lymph node disease without airway obstruction, or uncomplicated pleural effusion and paucibacillary non-cavitary disease confined to one lobe without a miliary pattern. A child who does not meet that definition still gets the standard six-month regimen, or the longer regimen recommended for that form of severe extrapulmonary disease. Shortening treatment for the wrong child is not a smaller intervention, it is a different one.

posts.headline: Three checks before every maintenance dose of magnesium sulphate
posts.sub: Respiratory rate above 16 a minute, patellar reflexes present, urine output over 100 ml in the last four hours. Any one missing and the dose waits.
posts.caption:
The loading dose gets the attention. The maintenance doses are where harm accumulates, because magnesium is cleared renally and a woman who is oliguric will hold on to it.

The third edition of the FOGSI-GESTOSIS-ICOG good clinical practice recommendations on hypertensive disorders in pregnancy sets the condition plainly: the maintenance dose is given only if respiratory rate is above 16 a minute, patellar reflexes are present, and urine output has exceeded 100 ml in the last four hours. All three, before each dose, recorded.

Both regimens remain in use, the intramuscular schedule with a 14 gram loading dose and the intravenous one with an hourly infusion. Whichever is running, the pre-dose check does not change, and an absent reflex is a reason to stop and reassess rather than to push on.

posts.headline: Metformin can start at diagnosis, alongside lifestyle, not only after it fails
posts.sub: RSSDI 2022 says metformin can be initiated in combination with lifestyle intervention at the time of diagnosis, with HbA1c measured every three to six months.
posts.caption:
The old sequence, diet and exercise for three months, then review, then a drug, is not the only route the current Indian recommendation allows. The RSSDI clinical practice recommendations for type 2 diabetes state that metformin can be initiated in combination with lifestyle interventions at the time of diagnosis, with the other oral classes reserved for when metformin is contraindicated.

The target deserves the same care as the drug. An HbA1c below 7.0% minimises the risk of developing complications, but the document is explicit that a higher target may be considered where earlier attempts at tight control caused unacceptable hypoglycaemia, or where the person sitting in front of you is at high risk of it. Monitoring runs every three to six months depending on the level, the stability of control and any change in therapy.

posts.headline: For persistent pain in a child, the strongest evidence is not a drug
posts.sub: WHO rates cognitive behavioural therapy and related approaches on moderate certainty evidence. Every recommendation in that guideline, the drugs included, is conditional.
posts.caption:
Chronic pain in childhood tends to be managed as a pharmacological problem, and the WHO guideline on the management of chronic pain in children does not support that ordering. Psychological management through cognitive behavioural therapy and related interventions, including acceptance and commitment therapy, behavioural therapy and relaxation therapy, may be used, and it carries moderate certainty evidence, the highest certainty anywhere in the document. Delivery may be face to face, remote, or a combination of the two.

Physical therapies may be used alone or with other treatments, on very low certainty evidence. Pharmacological management tailored to the indication may be used, on low certainty evidence. Morphine sits within end-of-life care, given by appropriately trained providers under the principles of opioid stewardship.

The caveat that matters: every one of these is a conditional recommendation, not a default, and the certainty labels are the reason why.

posts.headline: The second doctor to see a patient inherits the first one's diagnosis
posts.sub: Diagnostic momentum is how a provisional label hardens into settled history across a handover. Nobody re-examines the premise, because by the third telling it no longer sounds like a guess.
posts.caption:
A label picked up in a crowded casualty travels further than the reasoning behind it. By the time the patient reaches the ward, the working diagnosis has lost its question mark, and every subsequent decision is built on it. This is diagnostic momentum, and it is not a failure of knowledge. It is what happens when a summary is passed along faster than the uncertainty attached to it.

Two habits slow it down. When you hand over, say what the patient presented with and what you think it is, in that order, so the next clinician receives the findings and not only the conclusion. When you receive a handover, ask once what would have to be true for the label to be wrong, and check whether anyone has looked.

The patient who deteriorates on a confident diagnosis is rarely a patient nobody examined. Usually everybody examined them, for the wrong thing.

posts.headline: The clinical question is the most useful line on an imaging request
posts.sub: A request that says what you are trying to rule in or out gets a report that answers it. One that says only a body part gets a description.
posts.caption:
Radiology reads the request before it reads the images, and a request that carries a question performs differently from one that carries a region. Write the finding that worries you, the duration, and the decision the scan is meant to settle, and the report comes back addressing it. Write the body part alone and you get a careful description of everything present, which leaves you to work out which part of it mattered.

Three lines are usually enough. What the patient has, how long it has been going on, and what you will do differently depending on the answer. Add the relevant negatives and any previous imaging, because a comparison changes an interpretation more than any extra sequence will.

A vague request is not a smaller request. It is a slower one, and it often ends in a second scan.

posts.headline: Everything we publish is written for a clinician, not a patient
posts.sub: No patient photographs, no scan images, no before-and-after results, nothing that asks a patient to come in. The reader is the person who has to make the decision.

It is worth saying plainly who these cards are for, because it decides what we will and will not put on them. The reader we write for is a practising clinician deciding something this week. That is why a card carries a threshold, a caveat and the guideline it came from, rather than reassurance.

It also decides what stays off. We do not publish patient photographs or scan images. We do not publish before-and-after results, however good the result was. And we do not write anything designed to bring patients through a door, because a professional audience is owed information and not persuasion.

The narrower audience costs us reach. It is the right trade, and it is the only way a card is worth trusting when the clinical detail on it is the part that matters.

posts.headline: A consent form is the record of a conversation, not a substitute for one
posts.sub: The test of consent is not whether the sheet is signed. It is whether the patient can say back to you, in their own words, what could go wrong and what happens if they decline.
posts.caption:
The form protects the patient only to the extent that the conversation behind it happened. A signature collected on a trolley, minutes before a procedure, from someone who has already been told the decision is made, records compliance rather than agreement.

What makes the difference is asking the patient to say it back. Not a quiz, just an invitation: tell me what you understood, and what worries you most about it. The gaps that surface in that answer are the ones that turn into complaints later, and they take a minute to close. Cover what the alternatives are, including doing nothing for now, and write down the specific risks you actually discussed rather than the generic list.

A patient who can explain the plan in their own words has consented. One who has only signed has not, whatever the file says.

posts.headline: Observation, touch, then questions: the sequence before an ayurvedic diagnosis
posts.sub: Trividha pariksha orders the examination before any formula is considered, and a BAMS curriculum teaches the order as deliberately as the content.
posts.caption:
Ayurvedic diagnosis is sometimes described from outside as matching a symptom to a formula, which skips the part that is actually taught first.

A BAMS curriculum opens with trividha pariksha, the three-fold examination: darshana, what is seen; sparshana, what is felt on touch; and prashna, what is learned by asking. The sequence is deliberate, observation before touch, touch before questioning, so that each step checks the one before it rather than repeating it. Only once this examination is complete does the reasoning move toward a formula.

Treating this as a checklist to rush through misses what it is for. It is how the system builds a diagnosis it can stand behind, not a shortcut to one.

posts.headline: Two drugs from two classes, not one, is now the default first step for hypertension
posts.sub: Reserve a single drug for low-risk grade 1 hypertension, patients above eighty, or anyone frail. Everyone else starts on combination therapy, ideally as one pill.
posts.caption:
A solitary first prescription used to be the default, with a second drug added only once the first proved insufficient. The ICMR standard treatment workflow for hypertension in adults reverses that order.

Combination therapy, two drugs from two different classes, is set out as the default initial pharmacological treatment for most adults with hypertension, preferably as a single pill rather than two separate ones. Monotherapy is kept for specific groups: low-risk grade 1 hypertension, adults above eighty years, and patients who are frail, where a gentler start matters more than speed.

The targets that follow are familiar, below 140/90 for most adults, below 130/80 where diabetes, chronic kidney disease or cardiovascular disease is already present, below 150/90 past eighty. What has changed is the first prescription, not the destination.

posts.headline: The hour that decides infection risk in an open fracture
posts.sub: Antibiotics given within an hour of injury matter more than which antibiotic is chosen. The aminoglycoside add-on applies to every type three fracture, not just the more severe ones.
posts.caption:
An open fracture is treated as an orthopaedic emergency the moment the skin is breached, and the clock that matters most starts at the injury, not at the operating table.

The ICMR standard treatment workflow for open fractures names early antibiotic administration, ideally within one hour of injury, as the single most important factor in reducing infection rate. A cephalosporin is the base antibiotic across every grade, type one through type three C. For type three as a whole, grades A, B and C alike, an aminoglycoside is added to that base, and soil contamination of any grade adds metronidazole. Antibiotics continue for three days after wound closure.

None of this works if the first dose waits for imaging, for the operating list, or for a full debridement plan. The sequence is antibiotic first, everything else after.

posts.headline: A normal-looking newborn can still need an emergency dextrose bolus
posts.sub: Blood glucose below 20 mg/dL is treated with an immediate IV bolus whether or not the baby looks unwell; waiting for symptoms risks the brain injury the treatment exists to prevent.
posts.caption:
A newborn with a low blood glucose but no jitteriness, poor feeding or lethargy is often watched rather than treated, on the assumption that a baby who looks normal can wait for a recheck.

The ICMR standard treatment workflow for neonatology sets a lower bound instead of a waiting period. A blood glucose below 20 mg/dL is treated as an emergency regardless of symptoms: an immediate intravenous bolus of 2 ml/kg of 10% dextrose, followed by a continuous infusion at 6 mg/kg per minute. The workflow states plainly that both symptomatic and asymptomatic hypoglycaemia can cause permanent brain damage, so the absence of signs is not a reason to wait.

Check the number before you check the baby's appearance. Below that threshold, the bolus comes first and the examination follows.

posts.headline: Most patients do not need to stop metformin before a contrast scan
posts.sub: The reflex to hold metformin before an iodinated contrast study applies only below an eGFR of 30, or after an arterial study with renal-artery risk.
posts.caption:
Reflexively stopping metformin before every contrast-enhanced scan is still common practice on many wards, even when the patient's kidneys are working normally.

The ACR manual on contrast media sets a renal-function threshold instead of a blanket rule. For intravenous iodinated contrast, a patient with an eGFR of 30 or above and no acute kidney injury does not need to discontinue metformin either before or after the scan. Only an eGFR below 30, or acute kidney injury, calls for holding the drug at the time of the procedure and for 48 hours after, with renal function confirmed before it restarts. An arterial study with a risk of renal artery emboli is handled separately, and metformin is stopped regardless of eGFR.

The question worth asking before the form is signed is the eGFR, not the drug chart.

posts.headline: Tranexamic acid for postpartum haemorrhage only works if it arrives within three hours
posts.sub: WHO's recommendation sets a hard timing window, not a preference: the benefit falls with delay and disappears after three hours from birth.
posts.caption:
Tranexamic acid has earned a place in most postpartum haemorrhage protocols now, but the benefit is tightly timed, not open-ended.

The WHO recommendation on tranexamic acid for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage sets the dose at one gram intravenously, given over ten minutes, as soon as possible once bleeding is recognised, with a second one-gram dose if bleeding continues after thirty minutes. The caveat that matters: it must be started within three hours of birth. Benefit falls with every interval of delay, and WHO advises against starting it beyond that window.

This is not a reason to wait for a diagnosis to firm up. It is a reason to have the drug, the dose and the clock written into the same checklist, so the decision to give it is made in the first few minutes, not the first few hours.

posts.headline: The relative risk reduction is the impressive number; the absolute one is the useful one
posts.sub: The same trial result can be described as a large relative effect or a small absolute one, and only one of those numbers tells a patient what to expect for herself.
posts.caption:
A therapy reported to cut risk by a large margin sounds decisive. Whether that is worth having depends on the baseline risk it is cutting from, and that number rarely makes the headline.

Relative risk reduction compares two risks to each other. Absolute risk reduction compares the outcome to the starting point. A drug that produces a large relative reduction in a rare event may still change very few outcomes in absolute terms, because the baseline was already low. The same relative reduction applied to a common, high-stakes event changes a great deal.

Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions, and a trial result is read correctly only when both are stated with the baseline risk alongside them.

The caveat that matters: a result presented in relative terms alone, with no baseline risk attached, cannot be converted into a decision for the patient in front of you.

posts.headline: A coronary diagnosis moves the LDL target in diabetes from under 100 to under 70
posts.sub: ICMR's standard treatment workflow sets this lower goal only where coronary artery disease is already documented.

Where coronary artery disease is documented, that target drops to under 70. The workflow does not extend this lower threshold to diabetic kidney disease, retinopathy or a stroke history on its own.

The caveat that matters: treating every patient with diabetes to the same lipid goal misses the ones who need a stricter target, and can over-treat some who do not. It is the coronary history on the chart, not the diabetes diagnosis alone, that decides which number applies.

posts.headline: A number needed to treat means little until you know what outcome it was built on
posts.sub: The same NNT can describe a cure, a day of pain relief, or a one-point drop on a ten-point scale.
posts.caption:
A number needed to treat, or NNT, is often quoted as though it settles whether a therapy is worth giving. On its own, it does not.

NNT answers how many patients must receive a treatment for one additional patient to benefit, compared with the comparator. It does not say how large that benefit is, how it was defined, or how long it lasted. A pain intervention with an NNT of four for a fifty per cent reduction in pain scores, and one with an NNT of four for complete resolution, are not the same claim, even though the number on the page is identical.

Reading an NNT well means reading the outcome it was built on in the same breath, not stopping at the number itself.

The caveat that matters: a small NNT attached to a trivial or short-lived outcome is not automatically a stronger result than a larger NNT attached to an outcome the patient would actually notice.

posts.headline: A mechanical heart valve is the reason to pick warfarin over a DOAC

The caveat that matters: it is the valve or the severe mitral stenosis that should decide the drug class, not convenience, and not the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation by itself.

posts.headline: A composite endpoint can move without its most important part moving
posts.sub: When a trial reports a drop in a combined outcome, the benefit can sit entirely in its softest component while death or major illness barely move.
posts.caption:
A composite endpoint bundles several outcomes into one number so a trial can report a result with fewer patients and in less time. Reported as one figure, a reduction in the composite is often read as if every component in it improved by a similar amount. It rarely works that way.

A composite built from death, heart attack and revascularisation can show an overall benefit driven almost entirely by revascularisation, a softer and more subjective outcome, while death and heart attack barely move. The headline result is accurate. What it implies about the outcome a patient actually cares about is not.

Reading a composite endpoint well means asking for its individual components before deciding what the result is worth to the patient in front of you.

The caveat that matters: a positive composite result reported with no separate account of its hardest component has not yet told you what it claims to.

posts.headline: A positive test means less when the disease it is testing for is rare
posts.sub: The same test, with the same sensitivity and specificity, yields a different post-test probability depending on how likely the diagnosis already was before it was ordered.
posts.caption:
A test's sensitivity and specificity do not change from one patient to the next. What changes is how likely the diagnosis already was before the test was ordered, and that pretest probability decides what a positive result actually means.

Order a highly sensitive test in a patient with a low pretest probability, and most positive results will be false positives, however good the test's published numbers look in a textbook. Order the same test in a patient whose presentation already made the diagnosis likely, and a positive result is far more trustworthy, even though nothing about the test itself has changed.

This is why a test ordered to confirm a strong clinical suspicion and the same test ordered to screen a low-risk patient are not doing the same clinical work, and should not be read the same way.

The question worth asking before trusting any result: how likely was this diagnosis before the test, and does the result actually move that number enough to change what happens next.

Giving the steroid does not substitute for having that newborn care in place. Where it is not available, the same recommendation points to a different decision: refer before birth, not after.

posts.headline: A trial that misses its primary endpoint can still produce a convincing subgroup result
posts.sub: Split a null trial into enough subgroups and one slice will cross significance by chance alone; the count of comparisons decides how much to trust it, not how striking the number looks.
posts.caption:
A randomised trial that misses its primary endpoint has not entirely failed to produce findings. Split the same dataset into enough subgroups, by age, sex, baseline severity, region or site, and at least one of those slices is likely to cross statistical significance purely by chance.

This is not evidence of a real effect confined to that subgroup. It is the arithmetic of multiple comparisons: each additional subgroup tested raises the odds that some comparison looks positive even when nothing in the underlying biology changed. A subgroup finding earns attention only when it was specified before the trial started, when it fits a plausible mechanism, and when another trial finds the same pattern independently.

The practical rule: treat a subgroup claim from a trial that missed on its primary endpoint as a hypothesis for the next study, not as a reason to change today's practice.

posts.headline: A hip fracture goes to theatre the day of admission, or the day after
posts.sub: NICE's hip fracture standard reserves delay for patients not yet medically fit for surgery, not for an open slot elsewhere on the list.
posts.caption:
A hip fracture is not a scheduling problem to fit around a theatre list; once a patient is fit for surgery, timing itself is the treatment decision.

NICE's hip fracture quality standard QS16, drawing on guideline CG124, states that adults with a hip fracture should have surgery on a planned trauma list on the day of, or the day after, admission. The caveat that matters is what counts as a reason to wait. The standard's concern is avoiding unnecessary delay for patients already assessed as fit for surgery, not a routine pause while a theatre slot clears elsewhere on the list. A correctable medical problem, one that needs treatment before anaesthesia is safe, is a legitimate reason to wait a day. A gap in the list is not.

That distinction is the point of the standard. It does not ask every hip fracture to be rushed to theatre regardless of fitness; it asks that fitness, once established, stop being the reason surgery slips to day three or four.

posts.headline: A 6-8 mm solid lung nodule gets a stricter recheck schedule in a high-risk patient
posts.sub: Fleischner Society's 2017 criteria make a further scan at eighteen to twenty-four months optional in a low-risk patient and required in a high-risk one.
posts.caption:
An incidentally found solid pulmonary nodule on a scan ordered for something else does not call for the same follow-up in every patient.

The Fleischner Society's 2017 guideline splits a single solid nodule between six and eight millimetres by risk category. In a low-risk patient, the path is a scan at six to twelve months, with a further scan at eighteen to twenty-four months left to the radiologist's judgement rather than fixed. In a high-risk patient, that second scan at eighteen to twenty-four months is part of the recommended pathway, not an optional extra. Under six millimetres in a low-risk patient, no routine follow-up is needed at all; above eight millimetres, the next step is a scan, PET scan, or tissue sampling at three months, for either risk group.

The guideline carries a caveat worth checking first: it does not extend to a nodule found on a screening scan, an immunosuppressed patient, or someone with a known primary cancer, and it is not written for patients under thirty-five.

Risk category decides the pathway here as much as size does.

posts.headline: A newborn who is just not right is already showing a symptom
posts.sub: Feeding, colour, tone and activity often change before any single vital sign does, which is why a non-specific description still counts as a clinical finding.
posts.caption:
Neonatal illness rarely announces itself with one abnormal number on a chart. More often it shows up first as a change in feeding, colour, tone, activity or cry, each one unremarkable alone but worth noticing together.

Calling a baby just not right is sometimes dismissed as an imprecise handover, something to tidy up before it reaches a note. In a newborn, that description is frequently the earliest form an illness takes, arriving well before any single vital sign crosses a threshold a monitor would flag.

The caveat that matters is who is allowed to raise it. A parent's report that their baby is feeding differently or crying differently today deserves the same weight as a nurse's observation, because both are describing the same change from baseline, only from a different vantage point.

A vague description is not a weak one; it may be the first sign available.

posts.headline: Severe cancer pain does not have to start on a weak analgesic
posts.sub: WHO's 2018 guideline treats the three-step ladder as a general guide, not a protocol: the opioid matched to severity can be the first drug given.
posts.caption:
Ask a ward team how severe cancer pain gets treated and the answer is usually a ladder: a mild analgesic first, then a weak opioid, then a strong one, each step earning the next.

WHO's 2018 guideline on the pharmacological management of cancer pain treats that three-step ladder as a general guide rather than a protocol to climb. Paracetamol, an NSAID and an opioid may all be used at initiation, alone or combined, chosen by the severity of the pain assessed in front of you. For pain already moderate or severe, a mild analgesic alone should not be the first prescription; an opioid matched to that severity can be started directly, often alongside a non-opioid.

The caveat that matters: there is no fixed dose. The correct dose is the one that relieves that patient's pain to a level they find acceptable, reached by gradual titration and checked at regular intervals, because response varies by patient and by medicine.

posts.headline: Type 2 diabetes treatment escalates by HbA1c band, not by time on one drug
posts.sub: ICMR's standard treatment workflow adds a second agent once HbA1c sits between 8.5% and 10%, and allows a higher-than-7% target in elderly or significantly comorbid patients.
posts.caption:
Many wards still step up diabetes treatment the way they step up antibiotics: give the current drug a few months, review, then add another if the numbers have not moved.

ICMR's standard treatment workflow for type 2 diabetes sets the escalation by HbA1c band instead. Below 8.5%, metformin alone is the starting point. Once HbA1c sits between 8.5% and 10%, dual therapy begins: metformin plus a sulfonylurea, TZD, DPP-4 inhibitor, SGLT2 inhibitor, alpha-glucosidase inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist. Above 10%, the workflow offers two paths: basal insulin together with metformin and a further oral agent, or a triple oral-agent combination instead of starting insulin.

The caveat that matters: the usual target of 7% or below is not universal. The workflow allows a higher target in elderly patients and those with significant comorbid conditions, where tighter control can cost more than it gives back.

posts.headline: No difference in a trial often means not enough patients, not no effect
posts.sub: A trial underpowered to detect a real difference will report none, and that result is often read as reassurance rather than as a question about sample size.
posts.caption:
A clinical trial that finds no significant difference between two treatments is often read as proof the two work equally well. That reading skips a step worth checking first: whether the trial enrolled enough patients to detect a difference if one truly existed.

An underpowered trial and a genuinely negative one can produce a similar looking result on the page, but they say different things. The underpowered trial's confidence interval is wide enough to include both a meaningful benefit and a meaningful harm; a truly negative trial's interval sits tightly around no effect at all.

Before treating a null result as settled, look at the width of that interval, not only at whether it crosses the line of no effect. A wide interval around nothing is not evidence of nothing; it is a question the trial was never large enough to answer.

posts.headline: Analysing by intention to treat keeps a trial's comparison fair
posts.sub: A patient who switches treatment, stops early or is lost to follow-up still stays in the group they were first assigned to.
posts.caption:
A randomised trial starts as a fair comparison because treatment is assigned by chance, not by anything about the patient. That fairness only survives to the final analysis if every patient is counted in the group they were originally assigned to, whatever happened afterward, which is what an intention-to-treat analysis does.

A per-protocol analysis instead counts only the patients who actually completed the treatment as planned. That can look like the stricter, cleaner comparison, but it quietly drops the patients who stopped early because of side effects, who switched arms, or who did not tolerate the regimen, and those patients are rarely a random slice of the trial. Dropping them in one arm and not the other reopens the very bias randomisation was meant to close.

Reading a trial, check which analysis is reported as the primary one. A result that only holds up per protocol, and not by intention to treat, is telling you something about tolerability, not only about efficacy.

#CME #MedEd #EvidenceLiteracy

posts.headline: Don't de-escalate antiplatelet therapy in the first month after a coronary event
posts.sub: The 2023 ESC acute coronary syndrome guideline advises against stepping down from standard dual antiplatelet therapy during this early window, even when bleeding risk looks high.
posts.caption:
After an acute coronary syndrome, the instinct once bleeding risk looks high is to lighten the antiplatelet regimen early. The 2023 ESC guideline for acute coronary syndromes pushes back on that instinct for the first thirty days.

Its recommendation against de-escalating antiplatelet therapy in this window carries a class III caution, meaning the evidence does not support stepping down to a single agent or a less potent P2Y12 inhibitor that early, however appealing it looks on paper. The ischaemic risk in the first month after a coronary event stays high enough that the usual bleeding-risk argument for lightening treatment does not yet apply.

The caveat that matters: this caution is specific to the first thirty days, not a verdict on every later decision in the same patient. What the guideline rules out is stepping down inside that window, while the risk the second agent is protecting against has not yet fallen.

posts.headline: A surrogate endpoint moving does not mean the outcome that matters moved too
posts.sub: A drug can lower a lab value or shrink a tumour on a scan and still fail to reduce death, stroke or disability, which is what the surrogate was meant to predict.
posts.caption:
A trial can report success and still not have helped a single patient feel or live better. That gap shows up whenever the primary result is a surrogate: a stand-in measurement, such as a tumour's size on a scan, a lab value, or a narrowing seen on angiography, chosen because it is faster and cheaper to measure than the outcome a patient actually cares about.

A surrogate earns its place only when it has been shown, across many trials, to move in step with that real outcome. Several that looked biologically obvious have failed this test: improving one marker has, in specific drug classes, left death and major cardiovascular events unchanged, or made them worse, despite the marker itself moving exactly as intended.

Before treating a positive surrogate result as a reason to prescribe, ask what hard outcome the surrogate is meant to stand in for, and whether that particular drug class has actually been shown to move it. A tidier number on a report is not the same as a patient living longer or better.

#CME #MedEd #SurrogateEndpoints

posts.headline: Screening for gestational diabetes does not need a fasting test
posts.sub: The FOGSI practice recommendation allows a single glucose test, fasting or not, with a 2-hour plasma reading of 140 mg/dL or higher as the cut-off for gestational diabetes.
posts.caption:
Gestational diabetes screening does not need a fasting sample. The ICOG/FOGSI good clinical practice recommendation on GDM endorses the DIPSI single-step test: a 75 g glucose load dissolved in about 300 mL of water, taken fasting or non-fasting, with the timing of the last meal not mattering at all.

Plasma glucose is checked once, two hours after the load, using a plasma-calibrated glucometer. A reading of 140 mg/dL or higher is the cut-off for diagnosing gestational diabetes, and the protocol does not call for a second confirmatory test before starting management.

The caveat that matters: a negative result is not a one-time clearance. The same test is repeated between 24 and 28 weeks, at least four weeks after the first, because risk rises as pregnancy progresses. And if vomiting occurs within thirty minutes of the glucose load, the test is invalid and has to be repeated the next day.

#CME #MedEd #GDM

posts.headline: Acute low back pain without red flags does not need an x-ray or MRI
posts.sub: NICE reserves routine imaging for suspected infection, cancer, trauma, cord compression, inflammatory disease or cauda equina syndrome; most uncomplicated back pain settles within six weeks.
posts.caption:
A patient walks in with acute low back pain, and often the first question is which scan to order. For most of them, the guideline's answer is none.

NICE recommends against routine imaging in a non-specialist setting for low back pain, with or without sciatica, when there are no red flags and no suspected serious underlying pathology on history and examination. The reasoning holds up: most uncomplicated back pain resolves within six weeks on its own, and a scan rarely changes that course.

The caveat that decides when this stops applying: suspected infection, cancer or spinal metastases, spinal injury, cord compression, inflammatory conditions including spondyloarthritis in adults over sixteen, and cauda equina syndrome, where imaging should never be delayed. Any one of these moves a patient out of the reassurance-and-review path and into same-day imaging.

posts.headline: Bronchiolitis does not improve faster with a bronchodilator or an antibiotic
posts.sub: IAP's review finds no benefit from salbutamol, nebulised adrenaline, steroids or antibiotics in bronchiolitis, and flags a potential for harm in using them routinely.
posts.caption:
A wheezy infant with bronchiolitis often meets the same reflex: try a nebuliser, start an antibiotic just in case, see if the chest clears faster. The evidence points the other way.

The Indian Academy of Pediatrics' review of bronchiolitis management finds no benefit from salbutamol, nebulised adrenaline, glucocorticosteroids or antibiotics, and states that inhaled bronchodilators and these other therapies are not routinely recommended. It goes further: these interventions carry a potential for harm rather than a neutral one.

The caveat that matters: bronchiolitis in infancy is overwhelmingly a self-limited viral illness, and the therapy that actually helps is supportive, oxygen and fluids where needed, not a drug chosen to feel like something was done.

posts.headline: HbA1c below 7% is a starting point, not a fixed rule
posts.sub: The 2022 RSSDI clinical practice recommendations individualize the HbA1c target based on patient age, hypoglycemia risk, comorbidities and diabetes duration — and advise revisiting it if the target is missed on two consecutive readings.
posts.caption:
Type 2 diabetes | HbA1c management

The 2022 RSSDI clinical practice recommendations set HbA1c below 7.0% as the reference target for most adults with type 2 diabetes, with the explicit instruction to individualize it. A lower target may be appropriate when it can be reached safely without hypoglycemia. A higher target is the right choice for patients with significant comorbidities, advanced age, a long duration of diabetes, or a history of severe hypoglycemic events.

The caveat that matters: any agreed target should be re-examined if it is not met on two consecutive occasions. That is when the treatment plan needs to change, not when a single reading comes in high. HbA1c measurement is recommended every three to six months throughout.

The number is a threshold to check against, not a target to chase at the cost of the patient in front of you.

#CME #MedEd #DiabetesManagement

posts.headline: A non-inferiority trial sets the floor, not the ceiling
posts.sub: When a trial is designed to show a new treatment is 'not much worse' than the standard, the margin of acceptable inferiority is a clinical judgment built into the protocol before a single patient is enrolled.
posts.caption:
Clinical trial literacy | cross-specialty

A non-inferiority trial does not ask whether a new treatment is better than the comparator. It asks whether the new treatment is no worse than the comparator by more than a pre-specified amount, called the non-inferiority margin.

That margin is set by the trialists before the study begins, and it represents the largest performance gap they consider acceptable in clinical practice. The question to ask as a reader is whether you agree with that judgment. A margin that was chosen to make the trial easier to pass does not establish clinical equivalence; it establishes only that the new treatment fell within the chosen boundary.

A drug approved on non-inferiority evidence is not the same as a drug proved equivalent. It is a drug that failed to exceed the agreed floor. In some situations that is enough. In others, the floor matters a great deal.

#CME #MedEd #TrialDesign

posts.headline: Start high-intensity statins and ezetimibe together from day one after ACS
posts.sub: The 2024 CSI clinical practice guidelines recommend combining a high-intensity statin with ezetimibe at initiation of treatment after an acute coronary syndrome to reach an LDL target of below 55 mg/dL as early as possible.
posts.caption:
Cardiology | post-ACS lipid management

After an acute coronary syndrome, the 2024 Cardiological Society of India clinical practice guidelines do not recommend starting a statin alone and adding ezetimibe only if the LDL target is missed. They recommend combination therapy from the start.

The target is LDL below 55 mg/dL. Achieving it requires high-intensity statin therapy combined with ezetimibe at initiation, rather than a staged approach that requires a follow-up reading and a second prescription. If the target is still not reached after four weeks on this combination, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid or inclisiran are the next options.

The caveat that matters: the four-week review is built into the guideline. The combination is the starting point, not the ceiling. Patients who have high baseline LDL or cannot tolerate maximum statin doses will need that review and the escalation it may trigger.

posts.headline: Every All India CME session is built around a single clinical skill
posts.sub: The programme is not a series of talks on a topic — it is twenty-four sessions across a year, each one designed to move the same skill forward by one measurable step.
posts.caption:
A session in this programme does not exist to cover ground. It exists to move a skill.

The masterclass format means one clinical competency, selected because it matters in real practice, is taught across twenty-four sessions over a year. Each session has the same objective: make the participant marginally more capable of applying that skill than they were before it started. Not more informed. More capable.

That distinction shapes how the sessions are built. Information presented as a lecture moves understanding. A session built to change practice has to include the moment where the participant uses the skill under some form of constraint — a case, a question, a decision that must be justified — and gets feedback on whether they got it right.

This is CME in masterclass format. The masterclass is how the CME is taught. The CME is the point.

posts.headline: The tagline describes a standard, not a feeling
posts.sub: Uniform Excellence in Clinical Practice means every participant in the programme, regardless of location or seniority, encounters the same clinical standard in the same session delivered the same way.
posts.caption:
Uniform Excellence in Clinical Practice is not a phrase chosen for how it sounds. It describes a specific commitment.

Every session in this programme is delivered the same way to every cohort. The content is the same. The cases are the same. The standard against which a participant's answer is assessed is the same. A doctor in a tier-three city sits through the same session, with the same rigor, as one in a metro teaching hospital.

That uniformity is harder to achieve than it sounds. It requires a session to be built rather than performed, assessed the same way each time it runs, and checked against the same clinical standard regardless of who is in the room. It does not depend on a particularly effective facilitator on a particular evening.

The point of the standard is that it does not vary with circumstances it cannot control.

posts.headline: Relative risk reduction always looks larger than absolute risk reduction
posts.sub: A trial that cuts a 2% event rate to 1% can report either a 50% relative risk reduction or a 1% absolute risk reduction — both are correct, and only one of them tells you how many patients you need to treat.
posts.caption:
Clinical trial literacy | cross-specialty

The same result looks different depending on how it is expressed. A trial that reduces event rates from 2% to 1% can honestly report a fifty percent relative risk reduction. It can just as honestly report a one percent absolute risk reduction. Both numbers describe the same finding.

Relative risk reduction compares the two rates to each other: one percent is half of two percent. Absolute risk reduction compares them to a fixed baseline: one percent minus two percent is one percentage point. The number needed to treat — the inverse of the absolute risk reduction — in this case is a hundred patients to prevent one event.

The relative figure is the one that appears in most press releases and most headlines. It is larger, and larger looks more significant. The absolute figure, and the number needed to treat derived from it, is what belongs in a clinical decision.

Neither number is wrong. One of them is more useful.

posts.headline: Preeclampsia without severe features is managed until 37 weeks, then delivered
posts.sub: FOGSI guidelines recommend delivery at 37 weeks for preeclampsia without severe features, with a blood pressure target below 160/110 mmHg and fluid restriction at 80 mL per hour throughout to prevent pulmonary oedema.
posts.caption:
Obstetrics and gynaecology | preeclampsia management

For preeclampsia without severe features, FOGSI guidelines recommend expectant management until 37 weeks of gestation, at which point delivery is indicated. The goal of that management is BP control, not resolution — antihypertensives are titrated to keep blood pressure below 160/110 mmHg, a threshold that reflects the risk of stroke rather than an optimal target for the mother.

Fluid management is constrained. The guideline advises restricting IV fluids to 80 mL per hour, or 1 mL per kilogram per hour, specifically to reduce the risk of pulmonary oedema, a serious and preventable complication in preeclampsia.

The caveat that decides when expectant management ends: severe disease, eclampsia, or any deterioration in maternal or fetal status requires delivery regardless of gestation, after initial stabilisation. Thirty-seven weeks is the planned endpoint for uncomplicated disease, not the threshold for proceeding under pressure.

posts.headline: An AYUSH session reaches more learners when delivered in the learner's language
posts.sub: Sessions for AYUSH cohorts are delivered in the language the participants actually work in, which means regional-language delivery is built into the programme structure rather than added as an afterthought.
posts.caption:
A CME session delivered in a language the participant is not fully comfortable in does not teach what it sets out to teach. The content may be correct and the faculty expert, but the cognitive load of following unfamiliar language competes with the cognitive load of learning.

For AYUSH cohorts, the programme plans for regional-language delivery as a structural decision, not a concession to access. The session is designed to run in the language the participants actually read, document and communicate in, which is typically not English.

That has one practical implication that is easy to overlook: the cases, the clinical vocabulary and the assessment questions all have to be prepared in that language, not translated from an English original on the day. A translated session is not the same as a session built in the language. The difference shows up in the assessment.

posts.headline: Number needed to treat puts absolute risk reduction into clinical terms
posts.sub: NNT is the inverse of the absolute risk reduction, and it tells you how many patients need to receive a treatment for one to benefit — a figure that is useful for weighing benefit against cost, burden or side effects.
posts.caption:
Clinical trial literacy | cross-specialty

Number needed to treat is not a separate statistic. It is the absolute risk reduction expressed as the number of patients treated rather than as a percentage.

If a treatment reduces the absolute risk of an outcome from 4% to 2%, the absolute risk reduction is 2 percentage points, and the number needed to treat is fifty: one in fifty patients who receive the treatment will have the outcome prevented. The other forty-nine receive the treatment and do not benefit from it — though they still take on its risks and costs.

That framing is useful because it makes the trade-off visible. A treatment with a number needed to treat of ten and a number needed to harm of a hundred has a clear margin. A treatment with a number needed to treat of two hundred and a number needed to harm of fifty does not. The clinical decision is the same in both cases, but only one of them looks unambiguous from the relative risk alone.

#CME #MedEd #ClinicalEpidemiology

posts.headline: Neonatal sepsis with red flag signs needs blood culture and antibiotics immediately
posts.sub: IAP guidance categorises neonatal sepsis by probability: red flag signs, two or more yellow signs, or specific risk factors in infants at or below 32 weeks indicate high probability and require immediate admission, blood culture and empirical antibiotics without waiting for results.
posts.caption:
Paediatrics and neonatology | neonatal sepsis

IAP guidance on neonatal sepsis works through a clinical probability framework. The assessment begins with red and yellow flag signs. A neonate showing red flag signs, two or more yellow signs together, or a specific set of risk factors at or below 32 weeks gestation falls into the high probability category. In that group, management does not wait for culture results.

The sequence is admission, blood culture, and empirical antibiotic treatment started immediately. Antibiotic duration is determined later by the culture and CSF findings, and typically runs between five and twenty-one days depending on the pathogen and site of infection.

The caveat that matters: the framework requires a systematic assessment of both red and yellow signs together, not a response only to the most obvious finding. A neonate with a single yellow sign and a significant risk factor has the same classification as one with multiple yellow signs, and the same urgency follows.

posts.headline: AYUSH cohorts run as a separate track built on the same clinical standard
posts.sub: The AYUSH track is not a modified version of the allopathic programme — it runs as its own curriculum, built separately, with own-discipline content and high-value allopathic subjects taught by faculty qualified in each.
posts.caption:
The AYUSH track in this programme is not constructed by simplifying the allopathic curriculum. It is built separately, from the objectives up.

Own-discipline sessions cover Ayurvedic or homoeopathic practice and are built and assessed against those curricula. High-value allopathic subjects — pharmacology, basic sciences, clinical skills that cross disciplinary lines — are taught in the AYUSH cohort by allopathic faculty qualified in that subject, in the language the learners use, with cases and assessments prepared for that audience.

The clinical standard applied to both tracks is the same: does the participant leave with a measurable improvement in a skill they can use? The content differs because the practitioners differ. The standard does not.

Running these as separate cohorts is not a compromise on quality. It is what makes quality possible across a genuinely diverse learner group.

posts.headline: Diabetes and established cardiovascular disease call for a BP target below 130/80
posts.sub: The 2023 InSH consensus guidelines for India set a blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg for patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease or established cardiovascular disease, provided the target is well-tolerated.
posts.caption:
Internal medicine | blood pressure targets in diabetes

For most adults with hypertension, the 2023 Indian Society of Hypertension consensus guidelines set an office blood pressure target below 140/90 mmHg. For adults with diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease or established cardiovascular disease, the target is tighter: below 130/80 mmHg, on the condition that this lower threshold is reached gradually and is well-tolerated by the patient.

For adults aged 80 years or older, the systolic target is below 140 mmHg, regardless of comorbidities.

The caveat that matters: the lower target in high-risk groups is a treatment goal, not a threshold to reach quickly. Abrupt reductions in blood pressure in patients with long-standing hypertension, particularly in older adults or those with established coronary disease, carry their own risks. The guideline's qualifier — provided it is well-tolerated — is not a footnote. It is a clinical instruction.
